pos: adj. (fixed in purpose; firm; the citizen who has already decided)
etymology: From Latin resolutus, the past participle of resolvere, to loose, to untie, and so to settle a question by taking it apart. Webster notes that the Latin adjective does not carry the English sense. English took the word from resolve: a question worked through, then a will fixed. A resolute man is not a man who has never doubted. He is a man who has finished doubting.
biblical_def: Resolute is the settled will that remains after the question has been decided. Daniel purposed in his heart before the king’s meat was set before him (Dan 1:8). Joshua did not leave the choice open for his own house: “as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD” (Jos 24:15). Ruth would not be turned back (Rut 1:16). Paul determined to know nothing among the Corinthians save Christ crucified (1Co 2:2). The three friends at the furnace were “not careful to answer” the king (Dan 3:16) — not careless, but already decided, so the threat had nothing left to negotiate. Peter states the limit of every lesser loyalty: “We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29). Scripture’s word for this estate is steadfastness: “be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord” (1Co 15:58). Resolve is the decision. Resolute is the man who keeps it when the cost arrives. In this ministry the word names the RESOLUTE Citizen: Responsible, Engaged, Steadfast, Obedient, Loyal, Upright, Trustworthy, Enduring. Those eight words are the duties, not a slogan. A man may be loud about his country and still fail the duties: irresponsible in his own corner, absent from his city, moved by pressure, disobedient to lawful authority, disloyal to his people, crooked where no one is looking, careless with his word, and quit before the work is finished.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines resolute as having a fixed purpose; determined; hence bold, firm, steady, constant in pursuing a purpose. He notes that the Latin resolutus has a different signification, and sends the reader to Resolve.
webster_full: RES’OLUTE, adjective. [The Latin resolutus has a different signification. See Resolve.] Having a fixed purpose; determined; hence, bold; firm; steady; constant in pursuing a purpose.
Edward is at hand, ready to fight; therefore be resolute.
scriptures: Dan 1:8

But Daniel purposed in his heart that he would not defile himself with the portion of the king's meat, nor with the wine which he drank: therefore he requested of the prince of the eunuchs that he might not defile himself.

And if it seem evil unto you to serve the LORD, choose you this day whom ye will serve; whether the gods which your fathers served that were on the other side of the flood, or the gods of the Amorites, in whose land ye dwell: but as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.
Therefore, my beloved brethren, be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord.
Act 5:29
Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men.
corruption_summary: Resolute has been cheapened into a mood, a brand, and a political costume — firmness with no prior decision, and no Lord over the decision.
corruption_paragraphs: The age uses resolute as a posture. A man is called resolute because he will not yield in an argument, because his jaw is set, or because a campaign needs a word that sounds like courage. Webster’s sense is narrower and better: fixed purpose, constant in pursuing it. Scripture is narrower still. Daniel’s purpose had an object — he would not defile himself. Joshua’s purpose had a Lord. A will fixed on the wrong object is not resoluteness. It is obstinacy.

The other corruption is the opposite: resolve as a January feeling that expires when the cost arrives. Daniel’s purpose was tested at the table, and again at the lions. The three friends were not careful to answer because the answer had already been given. A resolute citizen is not a man who feels strongly about public life. He is a man who has decided, under God, what he will not do and what he will not abandon, and who is still there when the writing is signed.
roots_summary: Latin resolvere, to loose and so to settle; English took the moral sense from resolve. The biblical estate is steadfastness and a purposed heart, not a Latin adjective invented for the feeling.
roots_lines: Latin resolvere (re + solvere) — to loosen, to undo, and so to settle a question by taking it apart.
English resolve — the fixed purpose that remains after the question is settled. Webster sends the reader here, not to the Latin adjective.
Hebrew sum / sim (H7760), in Dan 1:8 — Daniel set it upon his heart. The purpose was placed, not felt.
Greek hedraios (G1476) — seated, steadfast; Paul’s word in 1Co 15:58 for a man who is not moved off his place.
usage: A resolute man has finished the question before the threat arrives, as Daniel had purposed before the meat was offered.
The RESOLUTE Citizen is responsible, engaged, steadfast, obedient, loyal, upright, trustworthy, and enduring — eight duties, not a mood.
Firmness aimed at the wrong object is not resoluteness. It is a will that refused to be settled by the Lord.

pos: adj. (tried and found true; the Scottish form of proved)
etymology: Webster (1828) records proven as the Scottish form of proved, the past participle of prove, from Latin probare, to test, to find good. The English verb is the parent. To prove a thing is to put it to trial. Proven names the outcome of that trial, not a reputation claimed in advance.
biblical_def: Proven is what remains after a real test. Scripture’s verb is prove: God proved Abraham (Gen 22:1, the older English tempt meaning to try, not to entice). He invites Israel to prove Him in the storehouse (Mal 3:10). A renewed mind proves the will of God (Rom 12:2). Paul turns the same word inward: “Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith; prove your own selves” (2Co 13:5). The standing rule for every teaching is “Prove all things; hold fast that which is good” (1Th 5:21). A man is not proven because he says so. He is proven because the trial disclosed what was there, and what was there held. In this ministry the word names the P.R.O.V.E.N. course and the after-action review that follows it: Passionate for God, Repentant, Open, Victorious in body and spirit, Eternal in perspective, Networking as brotherhood rather than status. The acronym is a measuring stick for men who have been through the work. It is not a title a man awards himself. Make full proof of thy ministry (2Ti 4:5) is the apostolic charge: finish the trial, do not announce the result.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) does not give proven an English definition of its own. He records it as a word used by Scottish writers for proved. The parent verb, prove, is to try, and then to establish as truth.
webster_full: PROVEN, a word used by Scottish writers for proved.

PROVE, verb transitive. To try; to ascertain some unknown quality or truth by an experiment, or by a test or standard. To evince, establish or ascertain as truth, reality or fact, by testimony or other evidence. To experience; to try by suffering or encountering.
scriptures: Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.
Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith; prove your own selves. Know ye not your own selves, how that Jesus Christ is in you, except ye be reprobates?
But watch thou in all things, endure afflictions, do the work of an evangelist, make full proof of thy ministry.
Rom 12:2
And be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind, that ye may prove what is that good, and acceptable, and perfect, will of God.
corruption_summary: Proven has been turned into a marketing adjective — stamped on a method, a man, or a ministry before any trial has been run.
corruption_paragraphs: The age puts proven in front of products, programs, and personalities as a claim of trust. Webster’s parent verb will not allow it. To prove is to try, to ascertain an unknown quality by a test. A thing announced as proven before the test is a thing that has skipped the only step that could make the word true. The Scottish form does not change the grammar. Proven is a participle. Something had to happen first.

The pastoral damage is a man who wears the word as a rank. Scripture’s order is the reverse: prove your own selves; make full proof of thy ministry; hold fast only what survived the test. A course called P.R.O.V.E.N. is an examination, not a decoration. Passionate, repentant, open, victorious, eternal, and bound to brothers — a man can still fail the test at any one of the six. A man who will not be examined has not been proven. He has been advertised.
roots_summary: Latin probare, to test and to find good. Webster records proven as the Scottish form of proved. The biblical verbs are Hebrew bachan and nasah, and Greek dokimazo.
roots_lines: Latin probare — to test, to find good. The root of prove, probe, probation, and approve.
Webster (1828) — proven is the Scottish writers’ word for proved. It is not a separate virtue.
Hebrew bachan (H974) — to examine, to try, as metal is tried. The LORD searches the heart (Jer 17:10).
Greek dokimazo (G1381) — to test so as to approve. Paul’s word in Rom 12:2, 1Th 5:21, and 2Co 13:5.
usage: A man is proven by the trial, not by the title he prints under his name.

P.R.O.V.E.N. names six things a graduate must still let a brother examine: his passion for God, his repentance, his openness, his victory in body and spirit, his eternal perspective, and his brotherhood.
Prove all things, then hold fast. The second verb is not available until the first has been done.

pos: adj. and participle (accomplished; completed; a charge brought to fullness)
etymology: The past participle of fulfill, Old English fullfyllan, to fill full, from full + fyllan. Webster (1828): accomplished, performed, completed, executed. The English word is a tautology on purpose. Full, and filled. Nothing left empty that was supposed to be filled.
biblical_def: Fulfilled is the completed state of a promise, a charge, or a course. Christ is the great fulfillment: “I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil” (Mat 5:17). The saint is given a lesser, real echo of that verb. “Bear ye one another’s burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ” (Gal 6:2). A father’s charge is one of those assignments. He is not fulfilled because his children turned out well, or because he feels complete. He is fulfilled when the charge God gave him has been carried out: bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord (Eph 6:4), teach them diligently (Deu 6:7), and do not provoke them to wrath so that the nurture is undone (Col 3:21). In this ministry the word names the FULFILLED Father: Faithful, Understanding, Loving, Fun, Intentional, Listening, Leading, Encouraging, Discipling. Nine letters, one charge. A father who provides and never disciples has not filled the office. He has furnished the house. The feeling of fulfillment, detached from the charge, is a modern substitute. In Scripture the word belongs to work that was actually done.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines fulfilled as the participle: accomplished; performed; completed; executed. The parent verb is to accomplish, to perform, to complete what was promised or intended.
webster_full: FULFILL’ED, participle passive. Accomplished; performed; completed; executed.
FULFILL, verb transitive. To accomplish; to perform; to complete; to answer in execution or event what has been foretold or promised. To accomplish what was intended. To answer a design by execution.
scriptures: Mat 5:17
Think not that I am come to destroy the law, or the prophets: I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil.
Eph 6:4
And, ye fathers, provoke not your children to wrath: but bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord.
Deu 6:7
And thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up.
Gal 6:2
Bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ.
corruption_summary: Fulfilled has been moved from a completed charge to a private feeling — so a father can be told he is unfulfilled while the work sits undone, or fulfilled while he never did it.
corruption_paragraphs: The age asks whether a man feels fulfilled, and treats the answer as a verdict on his life. Webster’s participle will not carry that question. Fulfilled means accomplished, performed, completed, executed. It describes work, not mood. A father who has trained his children in the way, brought them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord, and borne their burdens has done a fulfilled work whether or not the culture calls his life meaningful. A father who feels complete and has not done the work has a feeling. He has not earned the word.

The other corruption is the self-fulfillment errand: leave the charge in order to find yourself. Scripture assigns the fullness the other direction. Christ fulfills the law. The saint fulfills the law of Christ by bearing burdens. The father fulfills his office by staying, teaching, and not provoking. Fullness is the result of a charge carried to the end. It is not a destination a man reaches by abandoning the people he was given.
roots_summary: Old English fullfyllan, to fill full. Greek plēroō, to fill up and to complete, is the New Testament verb behind Christ’s fulfilling of the law and the saint’s fulfilling of the law of Christ.
roots_lines: Old English fullfyllan — full + fill. Webster calls the compound tautological. The repetition is the point: filled until full.
Greek plēroō (G4137) — to make full, to complete, to accomplish. Christ’s word in Mat 5:17, and Paul’s in Gal 6:2.
Greek ektrephō (G1625) and paideia (G3809) — to nourish up, and the nurture of Eph 6:4. The father’s charge is formation, not provision alone.
Hebrew shanan (H8150), in Deu 6:7 — to whet, to teach diligently. The instruction is sharpened in, not mentioned once.
usage: Christ fulfilled the law. A father does not repeat that work. He carries the smaller charge he was actually given.
The FULFILLED Father is faithful, understanding, loving, fun, intentional, listening, leading, encouraging, and discipling.
A feeling of fulfillment that survived an abandoned charge is not biblical fullness. It is a mood using a word that belongs to finished work.

etymology: Webster (1828) traces real to Low Latin realis, and notes that Latin res and English thing coincide with the Hebrew word for a word, a thing, an event. Real means actually being, not fictitious; true and genuine, not counterfeit or affected. The opposite of real is fake.
biblical_def: Real is what is, as opposed to what is performed. Scripture does not use the English adjective as a technical term, but it spends whole chapters on the distinction the adjective names. A man can have a form of godliness and deny the power of it (2Ti 3:5). He can say Lord, Lord, and not do the will of the Father (Mat 7:21). He can proclaim his own goodness while a faithful man is hard to find (Pro 20:6). The real thing is the thing that exists when no one is scoring it: faith that works, love that bears, a house that actually serves the Lord. In this ministry the word names the R.E.A.L. M.A.N.: Reject passivity, Engage consistently, Accept responsibility, Lead courageously, Manage faithfully, Account accurately, Never quit. Seven duties, scored on what a man actually did in the past two weeks, not on his best intentions. A real man is not a brand of masculinity. He is a man in whom the assigned work is actually being done. Counterfeit manhood has the vocabulary and not the verbs.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines real as actually being or existing, not fictitious or imaginary; true and genuine, not artificial, counterfeit, or affected.
webster_full: RE’AL, adjective. [Low Latin realis. The Latin res and English thing coincide exactly with the Hebrew word for a word, a thing, an event.] Actually being or existing; not fictitious or imaginary.
True; genuine; not artificial, counterfeit, or factitious. True; genuine; not affected.
scriptures: Pro 20:6
Most men will proclaim every one his own goodness: but a faithful man who can find?
Watch ye, stand fast in the faith, quit you like men, be strong.
Jos 1:9
Have not I commanded thee? Be strong and of a good courage; be not afraid, neither be thou dismayed: for the LORD thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest.
He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much: and he that is unjust in the least is unjust also in much.
corruption_summary: Real has been captured by two opposite lies: the performance of authenticity, and the sneer that any fixed manhood is a costume.
corruption_paragraphs: One corruption makes real a performance. A man is praised for being real when he narrates his failure, refuses a standard, or confuses candor with repentance. Webster’s real is not exposure. It is actual existence, as against the fictitious and the counterfeit. A confession that does not turn is not more real than obedience. It is a counterfeit with better lighting.

The other corruption treats any definite manhood as play-acting, so that the man who rejects passivity and accepts responsibility is accused of performing a role. Scripture will not help that sneer. Quit you like men is a command, not a costume note (1Co 16:13). The R.E.A.L. M.A.N. letters are verbs: reject, engage, accept, lead, manage, account, and do not quit. A man is real when those verbs are happening. He is counterfeit when he has the words and the last two weeks are empty.
roots_summary: Low Latin realis, from res, a thing. Webster ties the Latin and the English to the Hebrew word that can mean a word, a thing, or an event. Real is what has actually occurred.
roots_lines: Latin res — a thing, a matter, an event. Realis means belonging to the thing itself, not to the story told about it.
Webster (1828) — actually being; not fictitious. True; not counterfeit or affected.
Greek alēthinos (G228) — true, genuine, the real article as against the copy. Used of the true God, the true light, and the true vine.
Hebrew emeth (H571) — firmness, faithfulness, truth. The real man is the faithful man of Pro 20:6, not the man who proclaims his own goodness.
usage: A real man is known by the last two weeks, not by the speech he gives about manhood.
R.E.A.L. M.A.N. means reject passivity, engage, accept responsibility, lead courageously, manage faithfully, account accurately, and never quit.
Authenticity that refuses a standard is not reality. It is a counterfeit that learned the word real.

pos: n. (the state of being acted upon; the refusal to move when the charge says move)
etymology: From passive, Latin passivus, capable of suffering or of being acted upon, from pati, to suffer. Webster (1828) marks passivity as little used, and defines it as passiveness: the tendency of a body to persevere in a given state, of motion or of rest, until another body disturbs it. In physics that is inertia. In a man under orders, it is a sin with a scientific name.
biblical_def: Passivity is staying as you are when God has already spoken. It is not rest, and it is not meekness. Meekness is strength under control. Passivity is strength that will not engage. Adam was with his wife when she took the fruit, and the text does not record a word from him until the deed was done (Gen 3:6). Aaron made the calf because the people pressed him, and called the resulting feast a feast to the LORD (Exo 32:4-5). Eli heard what his sons did, and his rebuke did not stop them (1Sa 2:22-25). Scripture’s opposite is the command to stand, to watch, to quit you like men (1Co 16:13), and the rebuke of the man who knows his lord’s will and does not do it (Luk 12:47). In this ministry the first letter of R.E.A.L. M.A.N. is Reject Passivity — leading, not waiting. A man who waits to feel ready has already chosen not to move. The body at rest stays at rest until something moves it. A Christian man is not permitted to be that body. God’s command is the force that is meant to move him. Waiting for a more convenient feeling is the drift.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) marks passivity as little used, and defines it as passiveness: the tendency of a body to persevere in a given state, either of motion or of rest, until disturbed by another body.
webster_full: PASSIV’ITY, noun. Passiveness, which see. [Little used.]
The tendency of a body to persevere in a given state, either of motion or rest, till disturbed by another body.
scriptures: Watch ye, stand fast in the faith, quit you like men, be strong.
Jos 1:9
Have not I commanded thee? Be strong and of a good courage; be not afraid, neither be thou dismayed: for the LORD thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest.
Neh 6:3
And I sent messengers unto them, saying, I am doing a great work, so that I cannot come down: why should the work cease, whilst I leave it, and come down to you?
Jas 4:17
Therefore to him that knoweth to do good, and doeth it not, to him it is sin.
corruption_summary: Passivity is now baptized as humility, as “not my place,” and as self-care — so a man can abandon a charge and call the abandonment virtue.
corruption_paragraphs: The age has several names for a man who will not move. He is easygoing. He is not controlling. He is giving her space, giving the children room, waiting on God when God has already spoken. Webster’s little-used noun is more honest. A body perseveres in its state until something else disturbs it. That is a law of matter. It is not a law for a steward. The corruption is the decision to treat a moral charge as if it were physics.

The church version is worse, because it borrows true words. Meekness, patience, and submission are virtues. Passivity uses them as cover. Adam’s silence in the garden was not submission to God. Eli’s soft word was not patience. A man rejects passivity when he leads without waiting to be asked, engages when the work is unimpressive, and refuses the story that someone else will handle what was assigned to him. Rest is a gift. Drift is a sin. The two are not neighbors.
roots_summary: Latin pati, to suffer, to be acted upon. Webster’s noun is physical inertia. Scripture’s indictment is the man who knows the good and does not do it.
roots_lines: Latin passivus, from pati — capable of suffering or of receiving action. The passive man is the man to whom things are done.
Webster (1828) — little used. The tendency to stay in the present state until another body interferes.
Greek mē poieō, in Jas 4:17 — the sin is not a wrong act. It is the good act left undone by the man who knew it.
Greek andrizomai (G407) — quit you like men, act like a man (1Co 16:13). The antonym of passivity is not aggression. It is engaged strength.
usage: Passivity is not rest. Rest obeys a command to stop. Passivity ignores a command to move.
The first letter of R.E.A.L. M.A.N. is Reject Passivity: leading, not waiting to be asked.
A man who calls his drift humility has renamed a sin with a virtue’s name.

pos: v. participle (joining into one; the first work of this ministry)
etymology: The present participle of unite, from Latin unire, to make one, from unus, one. Webster (1828): joining; causing to agree; consolidating; coalescing; growing together. Uniting is not standing near each other. It is being made one.
biblical_def: Uniting is the work of making many into one under Christ, without pretending the differences were never real. Paul begs the Corinthians to speak the same thing, with no divisions, and to be perfectly joined in the same mind and judgment (1Co 1:10). The Spirit’s assignment to the church is to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace (Eph 4:3) — keep it, because God has already made it, and men are always trying to spend it. The psalm calls that unity good and pleasant (Psa 133:1). Christ’s own prayer is that his people may be one (Joh 17:21). Uniting is therefore not a mood of niceness and not a merger of errors. It is the patient work of bringing brothers into one confession, one table, and one aim. This ministry takes the word as its first named work: Uniting, Serving, Mentoring, and Counseling. The order is deliberate. Men are not counseled well in isolation, and they are not served well as a crowd of strangers. Iron sharpeneth iron (Pro 27:17) only when the two pieces are brought together. A ministry that collects an audience and never joins the men has not begun its first work.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines uniting as the participle: joining; causing to agree; consolidating; coalescing; growing together.
webster_full: UNI’TING, participle present tense. Joining; causing to agree; consolidating; coalescing; growing together.
UNI’TE, verb transitive. [Latin unio, unitus.] To put together or join two or more things, which make one compound. To join; to connect in concord.
scriptures: Now I beseech you, brethren, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that ye all speak the same thing, and that there be no divisions among you; but that ye be perfectly joined together in the same mind and in the same judgment.
Eph 4:3
Endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.
Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!
Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend.
corruption_summary: Uniting has been redefined as the erasure of conviction — agreement purchased by saying less, believing less, and calling the result love.
corruption_paragraphs: The age hears uniting and reaches for the lowest common sentence. Drop the doctrine, soften the command, stop naming the sin, and the room gets quieter. That quiet is then called unity. Paul will not sign it. The unity he begs for is speaking the same thing, in the same mind and the same judgment. A room that agrees by refusing to say anything has not been united. It has been silenced.

The other corruption is the institutional version: unite the brands, keep the distinct errors, and call the letterhead a fellowship. Webster’s participle includes causing to agree and growing together. Growth together requires a common root. This ministry’s uniting is narrower and harder. It is men brought to one Lord, one word, and one another, close enough for iron to sharpen iron. Audience is not union. A mailing list is not a body.
roots_summary: Latin unus, one, through unire, to make one. The New Testament words are henotēs, unity, and katartizō, to join perfectly, as a net is mended.
roots_lines: Latin unire, from unus — to make one. Webster’s participle is joining, consolidating, growing together.
Greek henotēs (G1775) — oneness. Eph 4:3 tells the church to keep a unity the Spirit has already given.
Greek katartizō (G2675) — to mend, to fit together, to perfect. Paul’s word in 1Co 1:10 for a church perfectly joined.
Hebrew yachad (H3162) — a unit, together. The brethren of Psa 133 dwell as one, not merely in the same town.
usage: Uniting is the first named work of this ministry, because counsel and service both fail among men who have not been joined.
Unity that requires silence about the truth is not unity. It is a truce with error.
Iron does not sharpen iron across a crowd. The pieces have to meet.

pos: v. participle (working under another’s charge; the second work of this ministry)
etymology: The present participle of serve, from Latin servire, to be a servant. Webster (1828): working for; acting in subordination to; yielding obedience to; worshiping; also, performing duties. The range is the point. The same word covers the worship of God and the work done for a brother. Both are subordination. Neither is self-display.
biblical_def: Serving is work done under the will of another, and in the church that other is Christ. The Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many (Mar 10:45). Whoever would be great among the disciples must be their minister (Mar 10:43). Peter tells elders to feed the flock not by constraint and not for filthy lucre, but willingly and of a ready mind (1Pe 5:2). Every man who has received a gift is to minister it as a good steward of the manifold grace of God (1Pe 4:10). Serving is therefore not a temperament and not a department. It is the shape of Christian work. This ministry names it second, after Uniting and before Mentoring and Counseling: men are joined, then they are put to work for one another. The apostles refused to abandon the ministry of the word in order to serve tables, and they also refused to abandon the tables (Act 6:2-4). Both services were real. A ministry that will only preach, or only organize, has cut the work in half. Serving tables is the half that costs the hands.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines serving as the participle: working for; acting in subordination to; yielding obedience to; worshiping; also, performing duties.
webster_full: SERV’ING, participle present tense. Working for; acting in subordination to; yielding obedience to; worshiping; also, performing duties; as serving in the army.
The word covers worship and assigned duty in one participle. Both are subordination to a rightful head.
scriptures: For even the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many.
As every man hath received the gift, even so minister the same one to another, as good stewards of the manifold grace of God.
Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind;
Act 6:4
But we will give ourselves continually to prayer, and to the ministry of the word.
corruption_summary: Serving has been split into a paid helping profession on one side and a vague call to “give back” on the other — neither of them subordination to Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: One corruption professionalizes service until only the credentialed may do it, and the ordinary man is left as a client. Peter’s sentence runs the other way. Every man who has received a gift ministers that gift. The body is not a clinic with one practitioner and a waiting room. The other corruption sentimentalizes service into “giving back,” a debt paid to the universe, with no Lord named and no particular brother in view. Webster’s participle is working for someone, in subordination, yielding obedience. Service with no master is a hobby.

The churchly corruption is platform service: the work that photographs well and never touches a table. Christ gave his life. The apostles kept both the word and the tables. A ministry called to serve does the unimpressive assignment — the ride, the meal, the hour with a man who is not useful to the brand. Peter rules out serving for money and serving under compulsion. He asks for a ready mind, and that rules out the man who means to serve someday and never starts. Serving is present-tense on purpose.
roots_summary: Latin servire, to be a servant. The New Testament words are diakoneō, to minister, and douleuō, to serve as a bondservant. Christ uses both of his own work and of his people’s.
roots_lines: Latin servire — to be a servant, to be subject. Webster includes worship and assigned duty under one participle.
Greek diakoneō (G1247) — to wait at table, to minister. Christ’s word for his own coming in Mar 10:45.
Greek oikonomos (G3623) — a steward. 1Pe 4:10 makes every gifted man a steward of grace, not an owner of it.
Greek diakonia (G1248) — the ministry, whether of tables or of the word (Act 6). The dignity is in the assignment, not the visibility.
usage: Serving is the second named work of this ministry: men joined, then put to work for one another under Christ.
Every man who has received a gift is already assigned. He is not waiting to be made official.
Service that needs an audience has changed masters. The Lord who sees in secret is sufficient.

pos: v. participle (advising from the word; the fourth work of this ministry)
etymology: The present participle of counsel, from Latin consilium, a plan, a consultation, a body of advice. Webster (1828): advising; instructing; admonishing. The English word is not the modern clinical license. It is one man telling another the truth, with a plan attached, in time to be of use.
biblical_def: Counseling in Scripture is counsel given, not a session sold. The sweetness of a man’s friend is hearty counsel (Pro 27:9). Where no counsel is, the people fall, and in the multitude of counsellors there is safety (Pro 11:14). Purposes are established by counsel (Pro 15:22). Paul tells the church that its members are able to admonish one another (Rom 15:14), and he charges the mature to restore a man overtaken in a fault, in the spirit of meekness, watching themselves (Gal 6:1). The Lord GOD gives the tongue of the learned, to speak a word in season to him that is weary (Isa 50:4). That is the work: a word, in season, from a man whom God woke to listen before he spoke. This ministry names Counseling last of the four works — after Uniting, Serving, and Mentoring — because advice detached from a shared life is an opinion. Hearty counsel comes from a friend. The word of Christ dwelling richly is what the counsel is made of (Col 3:16). A ministry that replaces that word with a technique has changed professions. Advise, instruct, admonish. Webster’s three verbs are enough.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines counseling as the participle: advising; instructing; admonishing.
webster_full: COUNSELING, participle present tense. Advising; instructing; admonishing.
COUNSEL, noun. [Latin consilium.] Advice; opinion given upon request or deliberation. Consultation; deliberation. Prudence; deliberate examination.
scriptures: Pro 27:9
Ointment and perfume rejoice the heart: so doth the sweetness of a man's friend by hearty counsel.
Where no counsel is, the people fall: but in the multitude of counsellors there is safety.
Gal 6:1
Brethren, if a man be overtaken in a fault, ye which are spiritual, restore such an one in the spirit of meekness; considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted.
Isa 50:4

The Lord GOD hath given me the tongue of the learned, that I should know how to speak a word in season to him that is weary: he wakeneth morning by morning, he wakeneth mine ear to hear as the learned.
corruption_summary: Counseling has been fenced into a licensed clinical trade, and the church has often accepted the fence — so ordinary biblical admonition is treated as dangerous amateurism.
corruption_paragraphs: The age hears counseling and thinks of an office, an hour, a code, and a theory of the self. Some of that neighboring work is lawful in its own sphere. It is not what the English word meant, and it is not what Proverbs commands. Webster’s participle is advising, instructing, admonishing. Scripture expects that work from friends, from elders, and from a people in whom the word of Christ dwells richly. A church that will not admonish until a license arrives has abandoned a duty and called the abandonment humility.

The other corruption is counsel with no word and no friend. Technique replaces the Scriptures. The counselor does not consider himself, lest he also be tempted. The weary man receives a method instead of a word in season. Hearty counsel is sweet because it comes from a man who is in the same life, under the same Lord, close enough to smell the ointment of Pro 27:9. This ministry’s counseling sits last on purpose. Unite the men. Serve them. Mentor them. Then the counsel has a body to live in. Advice from nowhere is not counsel. It is content.
roots_summary: Latin consilium, consultation and advice. Hebrew etsah is counsel, plan, and the prudence that keeps a people from falling. Greek noutheteō is to admonish, to put in mind.
roots_lines: Latin consilium — a plan reached by consultation. Counsel is not a reaction. It is a considered word.
Webster (1828) — advising, instructing, admonishing. Three verbs, none of them a license category.
Hebrew etsah (H6098) — counsel, advice, plan. Pro 11:14 and Pro 15:22: without it the people fall and purposes are disappointed.
Greek noutheteō (G3560) — to put in mind, to warn, to admonish. Rom 15:14 says the brethren are able to do this for one another.
usage: Counseling, in this ministry, is the fourth work: a word in season from a brother, after the men have been united, served, and mentored.
Hearty counsel is sweet because it comes from a friend. Anonymous advice is a different product.
Restore in meekness, and consider yourself. The man who admonishes from above a fault has already left the text.
